text: A yield vault takes Lesson 16's manual loop — claim a reward, sell or re-stake it, repeat — and runs it on a schedule through a bot or keeper network instead of requiring you to do it by hand. You deposit once; the strategy harvests rewards periodically and compounds them back in automatically.

The vault doesn't invent new yield — it captures the compounding gap Lesson 15 already showed, that an infrequent manual claimer leaves on the table. On a 20% APR farm with $10,000, claiming monthly nets about $12,194 after a year; harvesting daily nets about $12,213 — a real but modest $19 gap, before fees.

That's why marketing about huge auto-compounding APY boosts deserves scrutiny: most of the gain at reasonable frequencies is small, and fees can easily eat it. The real value is automation, not a dramatically bigger number.

Instead of crediting your wallet every harvest, most vaults mint a share token at deposit and let the exchange rate between shares and assets rise as the strategy compounds. Deposit 1,000 tokens at a price-per-share of 1.00, and you get 1,000 shares. After six months, price-per-share might rise to 1.08, so your withdrawal value is 1,000 times 1.08, or 1,080 tokens.

You never claim anything along the way — the share price itself embodies the compounding. That's also what lets vault shares be freely transferable, or even used as collateral elsewhere, since the IOU for your growing position is just a normal, fungible token.

Two fee types sit between the strategy and you: a management fee, a small annual percentage regardless of performance, and a performance fee, a cut of actual profit, commonly 10 to 20%. Next: reward emission schedules, and how the tokens funding all of this actually get released over time.
